scope: Move beyond the enactment-reason summary by verifying the operative Law No.708 text, penalty linkage, amendment survival, repeal timing, and successor-law leads; preserve the unresolved 1961-06-21 teachers-organization-bill lineage question.

findings.claim: Law No.708 Article 13 itself prohibited teacher labor activity and collective refusal to teach across national, public, and private schools.
findings.evidence: National Law Information Center historical text states in Article 13 that teachers of national, public and private schools may not engage in labor movements and may not collectively refuse classes.
findings.significance: This replaces reliance on the enactment-reason summary with the operative statutory provision itself.

findings.claim: Article 13 was backed by a criminal penalty, not merely an administrative norm.
findings.evidence: Article 22(1)(3) punished violations of Article 13 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to one million hwan.

findings.claim: The teacher-labor prohibition survived the recorded 1962-1963 amendments to Law No.708 until the statute's repeal took effect.
findings.evidence: The official amendment record changes Article 19 in April 1962, deletes Articles 7-8 in September 1962, changes Articles 10 and 15 and deletes Article 16 in February 1963, and deletes Article 21 in April 1963; none of these recorded amendments alters or deletes Article 13. The repeal law took effect 1964-01-01.
findings.caution: This establishes statutory survival, not the frequency or manner of actual enforcement.

findings.claim: Law No.708 was structurally broader than teacher-union suppression and reorganized university appointment, faculty screening, private-school governance, school consolidation, and degree rules.
findings.evidence: Historical statutory text verifies Articles 3, 9-12, 13-22; School Reorganization Standards Decree No.283 explicitly implemented Article 3(2).

findings.claim: Several private-school governance provisions of Law No.708 formed a basic framework for the 1963 Private School Act.
findings.evidence: National Archives' Private School Act topic page identifies Law No.708 Articles 11, 12, 17, 18, 19 and 20 and states that these later formed the basic framework of the Private School Act.
findings.caution: Clause-by-clause migration still requires direct comparison with Law No.1362.

findings.claim: The 1961-06-21 교직단체법 became, merged into, or supplied Article 13 of Law No.708.
findings.evidence: Policy subject matter overlaps, but the June bill original and disposition record remain unavailable in this pass. No textual lineage is asserted.

findings.claim: Law No.708's repeal automatically restored the pre-1961 teacher-labor legal position.
findings.evidence: By 1963 the general public-service legal framework had separately developed restrictions on public officials' labor/collective activity; therefore repeal of the temporary education statute cannot by itself be treated as restoration of the 1960 legal regime.
findings.caution: Exact successor treatment for national/public teachers and private-school teachers must be separately mapped through the 1963 National Public Service Act, Education Public Officials Act and Private School Act.

adversarial_checks: Article 13's existence does not prove derivation from the June 1961 교직단체법.
A criminal penalty on the books does not prove a particular teacher-union defendant was prosecuted under it.
The phrase collective refusal to teach is narrower than all collective teacher activity and must not be silently expanded.
National/public and private teachers require separate successor-law mapping after repeal.
Law 708 repeal did not erase contemporaneous general public-service restrictions.
Private School Act framework continuity is supported by an official archival synthesis but still needs article-level comparison.
Institutional Ministry responsibility does not establish Minister Mun Hui-seok's personal drafting or instruction.
Supreme Council enactment does not establish Park Chung-hee personal directive without a decision record.
Later university histories can establish institutional effects but cannot substitute for cabinet/Supreme Council drafting records.
Law 708 must be versioned because Articles 7, 8, 10, 15, 16, 19 and 21 changed before repeal.
